name: Pedro Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking to me, Pedro. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. What you tell me is confidential. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My day starts at nine at night. I drive an articulated lorry on the trunk run for a supermarket chain, taking full trailers from the big distribution centre up north to the smaller one by the coast, then bringing empties back. It's about 220 kilometres each way, mostly motorway, and I'm home by six in the morning. I like the empty roads and the radio, and I hate the fog in February.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's life like outside the cab?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Lena, who's a nurse on a children's ward, so we see each other at breakfast and on weekends. We're careful with money. We've got about eight months of my pay saved and the car is paid off. I use a chatbot now and then, mostly to check my tax forms or plan a trip, but I'm not glued to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a lot of noise about nothing, and I'd be quietly glad. The lads in the canteen at the distribution centre would have a laugh about all the talk of lorries without drivers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I keep a good night job with a premium on top. Trunking pays well because nobody wants nights. My only real worry in that world is my back, because ten years of sitting in a seat at night isn't kind to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job and keep saving. I'd probably start going to a gym in the day, before my back makes the decision for me. Maybe I'd try the route-planning app the company keeps pushing, since it seems to save the day drivers some time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. It's not exciting, but it's a good wage and Lena's job is solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your back. Is that a bigger worry than AI right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, honestly. My uncle drove for thirty years and ended up with two discs fused. I'm twenty-seven and I already feel it after a long week. In the plateau picture, my body is the thing that ends my driving, not a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you change about money in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much. We'd keep saving and probably buy a flat in the next couple of years. Lena wants to be near her hospital, so we'd look on that side of town.

say: I'd say the AI talk was **mostly noise** and be quietly glad about it.
I'd laugh along with the **canteen crowd** about lorries without drivers.
think: I think I keep a **well-paid night job** with a premium most people don't want.
My real worry here is **my back**, not computers.
do: Keep the **night trunk run** and keep saving at the same rate.
Start going to a **gym in the day** to protect my back.
Try the company's **route-planning app** that day drivers already use.
feel: He feels **calm**, with a well-paid job and a partner in a steady job.
S0.quote: In the plateau picture, my body is the thing that ends my driving, not a computer.
fieldNote: His main pressure in this world is **physical wear**, shaped by an uncle with fused discs.
He's mildly open to the company's **route-planning app** once colleagues have used it.
Money feels **settled**, with a flat purchase on the near horizon.

steps.text: Keep driving the night trunk run and saving the night premium
Join a gym and train in the daytime to protect his back
Try the route-planning app the day drivers already use

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the drivers are fine for now, but the transport office will get a shake-up. Planning, booking slots at the gates, sorting the paperwork, that's exactly what the card says goes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be watching closely. Trunking is the easiest driving to automate. It's the same motorway every night, the same two gates. Robots are slower in this picture, but when they come, my run is the first one they'll want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start getting the skills for the messier work, the kind that's hard for a machine. I'd ask to do a few day shifts on city multi-drop, the deliveries to small shops, so I've got that on my record. I'd use the AI tools the company brings in, because if the planning is done by software, I'd rather understand it than fight it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not losing sleep yet, but I'd be reading every bit of news about driverless lorries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in the transport office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kev, who plans the night runs. He's the one I ring when a trailer isn't ready, and he sorts it in two minutes. If they replace him with a program, I'd be ringing a phone line at three in the morning. That worries me more than it sounds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move to messier work. Would that mean less pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd lose the night premium on day multi-drop, maybe a fifth of my wage. I wouldn't jump yet. I'd do a few shifts so I'm ready, but I'd stay on nights while the money's there.

say: I'd say drivers are fine and the **transport office** will feel it first.
I'd point out that **booking gate slots** and paperwork are exactly what goes.
think: I think **trunking** is the easiest driving to automate once robots arrive.
I'd miss **Kev the night planner**, who fixes problems in two minutes.
do: Ask for a few **day multi-drop shifts** to build experience for messier work.
Use the company's **new AI tools** rather than fight them.
Stay on **night trunking** while the premium lasts.
feel: He feels **uneasy** and would follow every story about driverless lorries.
S1.quote: Trunking is the easiest driving to automate. It's the same motorway every night, the same two gates.
fieldNote: He clearly sees his **specific route type** as the first target for driverless lorries.
He'd **hedge** by gaining city multi-drop experience without giving up night pay yet.
He values the **human planner**, which hints at fears beyond his own seat.

steps.text: Ask the supermarket depot for a few city multi-drop day shifts
Learn the new planning software the company brings in
Stay on the night trunk run while the night premium lasts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the one the government should have been planning for, and I'd say it loud. You can't have hundreds of thousands of drivers all looking for work in the same year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it means my run goes driverless around 2031, maybe 2032 if the rules are slow. Trunking is the first thing they'll do. I'd be thirty-two, still young, with savings, but I'd be one of a lot of drivers chasing the same few jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd move to day multi-drop within a year, even with the pay cut, because city deliveries with steps and shop doors will take robots longer. Then I'd start an evening course to become a heavy vehicle technician, since somebody has to service the driverless lorries. Lena and I would buy the flat now, while the bank still sees two wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I've got time and money to make a plan, and I'd make one, but the floor is moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the government should plan for it. What do you actually want them to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay for retraining for drivers before the robots arrive, not after. And put some rules on how fast a firm can swap a whole fleet. I'd write to my MP about it, which I've never done in my life. I'm not against the technology, I just don't want it all on one Monday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lena about money that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Lena we're fine for a year or two whatever happens, because we are. Then I'd say we should keep saving like I'm already out of work, just in case.

say: I'd say **government should plan** for hundreds of thousands of drivers at once.
I'd say I'm **not against** the technology, only against it arriving all at once.
think: I expect my **trunk run** to go driverless around 2031 or 2032.
At thirty-two I'd be competing with **many drivers** for the same few jobs.
do: Move to **day multi-drop** within a year, accepting a pay cut.
Start an **evening technician course** to service driverless lorries.
Buy **the flat now** while the bank sees two wages.
feel: He feels **anxious** but still in control, with time and savings to plan.
S2.quote: I'm not against the technology, I just don't want it all on one Monday.
fieldNote: His fear is **crowding**: thousands of displaced drivers chasing the same jobs at once.
He accepts a **pay cut now** to buy time on harder-to-automate city routes.
His politics are **pragmatic**, asking for paced change and retraining, not a ban.

steps.text: Switch from night trunking to day city multi-drop within a year
Enrol in an evening heavy vehicle technician course
Buy a flat near Lena's hospital while both wages count
Write to his MP asking for paid driver retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's enough warning for drivers to sort themselves out, if the firms are honest about their plans. I'd tell the younger ones not to get too comfortable on trunking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I've got until about 2034 on driving. The thinking AI in 2031 hits the office, not my seat. That's seven or eight years, which is enough to finish a technician course without rushing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on nights for now and bank the premium, and I'd start the technician course part-time around 2028. We'd buy the flat in a year or so as planned. I'd keep using the AI tools at work so I'm not behind when the new lorries come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than worried. It's a deadline, but it's a long one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a point where you'd move faster than that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the company starts testing driverless trailers on our motorway, I'd switch straight away. Before that, I'd rather earn the night money and save it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at the depot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older drivers in their fifties, with nothing else on their licence, will be the ones told they're too old to retrain. I'd try to get a few of them on the course with me.

say: I'd say there's **enough warning** for drivers, if firms are honest.
I'd tell **younger drivers** not to get comfortable on trunking.
think: I think driving lasts until about **2034** for me.
Seven or eight years is enough to **finish a course** without rushing.
do: Stay on **nights** and bank the premium for now.
Get **older drivers** to join the course with me.
feel: He feels **uneasy**, seeing a deadline but a long one.
S3.quote: The older drivers in their fifties, with nothing else on their licence, will be the ones told they're too old to retrain.
fieldNote: The longer timeline shifts him from **switching now** to earning and saving first.
He sets a clear **trigger**: driverless trailer tests on his motorway.
He shows **concern for older colleagues** without being prompted to.

steps.text: Stay on night trunking and save the night premium
Start a part-time heavy vehicle technician course in 2028
Invite older depot drivers to join the technician course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a whole career for some people, so there's no point panicking. I'd still tell people to learn a second skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, in ten years I'd probably have moved on from trunking anyway, because of my back. So this picture almost matches my own plan. I'd be about forty when the robots take the driving, with a flat mostly paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on driving and saving, and I'd use the time well. I'd take the technician course slowly, maybe one module a year, and try to move into the workshop by my mid-thirties. I'd keep trying the AI tools as they get proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like a normal working life with a turn in the middle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound relaxed. Is anything still nagging you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only one thing. Everyone will say ten years and then do nothing for nine. I'd want to be the one who started early. I've seen it happen with the fuel rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change plans with Lena?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, if anything it makes them easier. We'd probably think about kids in five years or so. A decade of warning means I can plan around it.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a whole career, so there's no need to panic.
I'd still tell people to **learn a second skill**.
think: I'd likely leave trunking anyway because of **my back**.
By about **forty** I'd have a flat mostly paid off.
do: Keep driving and **saving** at the usual rate.
Take the **technician course** one module a year, aiming for the workshop by mid-thirties.
feel: He feels **calm**, seeing a normal working life with a turn in it.
S4.quote: Everyone will say ten years and then do nothing for nine. I'd want to be the one who started early.
fieldNote: The decade lines up with **his own plan** to leave night driving for his back.
He's wary of **collective complacency** and wants to start early.
Family plans stay **on track**, with children possible in about five years.

steps.text: Keep driving the trunk run and saving as now
Take one technician course module a year aiming for the workshop

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Trunking would be the first to go, and every driver in the country would be looking for the same jobs at once. What would help is paid retraining that starts before the robots come, and a firm that tells us its plan honestly, two years ahead.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how the work feels at three in the morning. There's a kind of quiet trust between night drivers, flashing your lights to say thanks on the motorway. A robot lorry won't flash its lights at anyone, and I think we'll miss that more than we expect.

headlineQuote: A robot lorry won't flash its lights at anyone, and I think we'll miss that more than we expect.
portrait: Pedro is a **27-year-old night trunk driver** for a supermarket chain, living with Lena, a children's nurse.
He has **eight months saved**, uses chatbots now and then, and worries most about his back.
He's calm in AI Plateau but sees **trunking** as the first driving to go driverless.
In AGI by 2028 he'd take a **pay cut** for city multi-drop and train as a technician.
Longer warning lets him **bank the night premium** first and retrain at a slower pace.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** most, because trunk runs would go first and drivers would flood the market.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **paid retraining** that starts before robots arrive.
He wants his employer to share its **automation plans** two years ahead.
